newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Moroccans go to polls aimed at extending democracy.
newsitem.headline: Moroccans go to polls aimed at extending democracy.

text.p: Millions of Moroccans voted on Friday in local elections intended to give more powers to rural regions to improve living standards and lay the basis for wider democracy in the North African country.

With polling due to end at 6 p.m. (1800 GMT), numerous voting stations extended their hours until 8 p.m. (2000 GMT), to help maximise voting. The Interior Ministry said it had no figures on how many stations had shut or remained open and that the decision was taken by the president of the vote station.
An official added that at 4 p.m. (1600 GMT) turnout was 51.02 percent and voting had taken place in a completely calm atmosphere. More than 13 million people are eligible to vote.

"The local councils from now on will form the base of the national pyramid of democracy," the independent le Quotidien magazine said, referring to planned reforms under a constitution approved in September 1996.

King Hassan said last year on television that he was "fed up" with vote-rigging charges and he personally pledged honest elections. Opposition parties are going all out to try to change three decades of rule at all levels by pro-government parties.
Among early voters was Prime Minister Abdellatif Filali, who voted in Souissi near his home. Leaders of Morocco's dozen parties voted in Casablanca, Rabat, Marrakesh, Agadir and other cities.
Most of the parties are linked in three main alliances, the opposition Koutla, the pro-government rightist Wifaq group, and the centre-right group led by the Independent National Rally.
In a sign of the authorities' pledged "transparency", clear plastic ballot boxes were being used for the first time.

Later this year, under the new constitution, the 1,547 local councils emerging from Friday's vote will select three-fifths of the members for a new upper house of parliament. The country will then have two assemblies in place of the one 333-seat body.

"The importance of Friday's polls lies in the fact that future communal representatives will hold three-fifths of the upper house," said Mohamed El Yazghi, a leading figure of the opposition Socialist Union of People's Forces (USFP).

Under planned decentralisation, regional councils will also have greater finance and power to push development to end the disparity between town and country. This is reflected in higher illiteracy, poorer health and living standards for those living in the countryside -- about half the 28 million population.
More than 100,000 Moroccans are standing for around 25,000 seats in councils on which about 65 percent of seats were taken by pro-government and centre-right parties in a 1992 ballot.

At Lycee Moulay Youssef voting station near the Royal Palace in Rabat, one early voter, Fatima Hamdi, a teacher in her early 20s, said: "I decided to vote for the USFP because I want a real political change...My generation is fed up with right-wing parties running the councils since independence in 1956."

Around 15,000 independent candidates are also competing in the 16 provinces, including four in disputed Western Sahara, claimed and largely controlled by Morocco and where the Polisario Front is seeking independence.

The official Algerian news agency APS on Friday quoted a Front statement as criticising the vote as a "deliberation violation of the peace terms" at a time when the U.N. special envoy James Baker had just met opposing sides to try to advance a U.N. peace plan.
Some 1,600 women are standing, the official news agency MAP said on Friday. Earlier a senior official put the figure at 6,600.
Malika, a 40-year-old woman teacher casting her vote in Rabat, said: "I"ll vote for a woman. I expect her to be more honest."
